title: What a Closure Captures
goal: A closure borrows, mutably borrows, or takes ownership. Its body decides which.

sections.text: A closure is a function that can use variables from the scope around it. Capturing follows the weakest rule the body allows: reading a variable borrows it, mutating it borrows mutably, and consuming it takes ownership. You do not choose the capture mode; the body does.

sections.caption: A read-only body only borrows.

sections.text: The `move` keyword overrides the default and transfers captured variables into the closure. This matters when the closure outlives the current function, for example in a spawned thread. Watch the interaction with `Copy` types: `move` on an `i32` captures a copy, so mutating it inside the closure changes the copy, not the original.

Every closure implements one of three traits, based on what its body does to the captures. `Fn` closures only read and can be called any number of times. `FnMut` closures mutate and need a mutable binding to call. `FnOnce` closures consume a capture and can be called exactly once. The traits nest: every `Fn` is also `FnMut` and `FnOnce`. When a function takes a closure as a parameter, it should ask for the weakest trait its usage needs.

explanation: The body decides the capture: read borrows, mutate borrows mutably, consume takes. Fn, FnMut, and FnOnce name those three contracts.
